body:
What is rock-cut architecture?

Rock-cut architecture refers to buildings and spaces created by cutting and removing material from natural rock. Instead of constructing walls by joining bricks or stone blocks, artisans excavated the rock itself to form halls, rooms, pillars, doorways and sculptures.

The method is often described as subtractive construction: the desired space or building emerges as unwanted stone is removed. The remaining rock forms the walls, roof, pillars and other architectural elements. These monuments are therefore different from ordinary structural buildings assembled from separate materials.

India has a long tradition of rock-cut architecture associated with religious life. Some of the earliest surviving examples belong to the Mauryan period in the 3rd century BCE. Later, Buddhist, Jain and Hindu communities developed different kinds of rock-cut monasteries, prayer halls and temples.

Chaityas, viharas and cave temples

Although many rock-cut monuments are commonly called caves, they did not all serve the same purpose. Their arrangements reveal whether they were intended mainly for congregational worship, residence or the worship of a deity.

Chaityagriha: a hall for worship

A chaityagriha, commonly called a chaitya hall, is a place for religious worship or assembly. In early Buddhist rock-cut architecture, it usually contained a stupa at the rear. A stupa is a sacred mound or monument associated with the Buddha, his relics or his memory.

Many Buddhist chaitya halls have a long central space ending in a rounded or apsidal rear portion. The roof may be vaulted, and a large horseshoe-shaped or semicircular opening may appear above the entrance. This distinctive opening is called a chaitya arch or chaitya window. The architectural form is especially useful for recognising early Buddhist cave halls.

Vihara: a residence for monks

A vihara is a monastery or monastic residence. In a common rock-cut arrangement, small cells open into a larger hall. Monks used these cells for residence and meditation. Many viharas also had verandas and pillared halls.

In later Buddhist excavations, a vihara could contain a shrine with an image of the Buddha. Therefore, the presence of a Buddha image does not automatically mean that the whole cave was originally designed as a chaitya hall.

Rock-cut temple and monolithic temple

A rock-cut cave temple is excavated into a rock face to create an interior sacred space. The cave temples at Badami are examples.

A monolithic temple is carved from a single continuous mass of rock so that the remaining stone resembles an independent building. The Five Rathas at Mahabalipuram and the Kailasa Temple at Ellora demonstrate this form. Monolithic does not mean that the monument was assembled from many stone blocks.

Chaitya, vihara and monolith

  • Chaitya hall: primarily a worship or assembly hall, commonly with a stupa in early Buddhist examples.
  • Vihara: primarily a monastic residence, often with cells around a central hall.
  • Monolithic temple: a temple formed by carving one continuous body of natural rock.

Why different religious traditions used rock-cut architecture

Rock-cut spaces provided places where religious communities could live, meditate and worship. Buddhist monks occupied viharas and assembled in chaitya halls. Jain monks also used rock-cut retreats and residential cells. Hindu patrons developed cave shrines and, later, remarkable monolithic temples.

These forms did not replace one another in a simple sequence. Caves and structural temples continued to exist together, and different religious communities sometimes created monuments in the same region. The arrangement of a cave and its sculptures must therefore be considered together before identifying its religious association.

Prelims focus

  • Rock-cut architecture is created by removing stone from natural rock.
  • A Buddhist chaitya hall commonly contains a stupa.
  • A vihara generally provides residential cells for monks.
  • Some of the earliest surviving rock-cut caves belong to the Mauryan period.
  • Mahabalipuram's rathas and Ellora's Kailasa are important monolithic examples.
  • Trap: Not every rock-cut cave is Buddhist, and not every Buddhist cave is a chaitya hall.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 12, Buildings, Paintings and Books, pp. 123–126; NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 4, Post-Mauryan Trends in Indian Art and Architecture, pp. 35–36; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Chapter 4, Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings, pp. 106–107.]

title: Rock-cut Architecture in India: Meaning, Types and Development

body:
The earliest surviving tradition

The Barabar Hills caves in present-day Jehanabad district, Bihar, are among the earliest surviving examples of India's rock-cut architecture. They belong to the Mauryan period, particularly the 3rd century BCE. The hills are near Gaya, which explains why older textbook descriptions often identify their location as near Gaya.

These caves were excavated in hard granite. Several interiors have remarkably smooth, polished stone surfaces, demonstrating the skill of Mauryan stoneworkers. The caves are especially important because their inscriptions connect early rock-cut architecture with identifiable rulers and religious communities.

Ashoka, Dasaratha and the Ajivikas

The Barabar caves are closely associated with Emperor Ashoka and the Ajivika sect. The Ajivikas were an ancient religious and philosophical community associated with Makkhali Gosala. They were distinct from both Buddhists and Jains.

Ashoka made caves available to Ajivika ascetics. An inscription in the Sudama Cave records an excavation during his 12th regnal year, conventionally dated to 261 BCE. This provides direct evidence of Mauryan royal patronage.

The nearby Nagarjuni Hills also contain Mauryan caves. Their patronage is associated with Dasaratha, Ashoka's grandson. An inscription at the Vadathika Cave records a donation by Dasaratha.

Barabar and Nagarjuni are closely related groups but should not be treated as the same hill. The commonly described complex has 4 caves at Barabar and 3 at Nagarjuni.

Lomas Rishi Cave: its distinctive entrance

The best-known architectural feature of Lomas Rishi Cave, also written Lomash Rishi, is its carefully carved entrance. Above the doorway is a large semicircular chaitya arch, recalling the shape of a wooden architectural opening. An ornamental frieze shows elephants approaching stupas.

The decoration demonstrates an important relationship: early rock-cut architects could reproduce shapes that had already developed in buildings made with other materials, particularly wood.

The arrangement of the cave

The cave contains a rectangular hall associated with a rounded inner chamber at the back. This combination of differently shaped spaces is characteristic of the early excavation.

The architectural significance of Lomas Rishi lies in its early date, distinctive entrance and use of a carefully planned interior. It should not be confused with the much larger Buddhist monastic complexes that developed in subsequent centuries.

A qualification about the inscriptions

The Mauryan patronage of the Barabar cave group is established by inscriptions at several caves. However, the surviving inscriptions recorded at Lomas Rishi itself are later inscriptions, dated to approximately the 7th–8th centuries CE. An Ashokan inscription at another Barabar cave should not be incorrectly assigned to Lomas Rishi.

Historical importance

Barabar demonstrates that royal patronage of rock-cut architecture began before the elaborate Buddhist cave complexes of western India. It also shows why the religion of a monument must be established from its history and inscriptions rather than from its appearance alone: a chaitya-like arch at Lomas Rishi does not make the cave a Buddhist foundation.

Prelims focus

  • Barabar Hills: Jehanabad district, Bihar; Mauryan rock-cut caves.
  • Ashoka: patron of caves associated with the Ajivikas.
  • Dasaratha: associated with the nearby Nagarjuni caves.
  • Lomas Rishi: semicircular chaitya arch and elephant frieze.
  • Sudama Cave: inscription referring to Ashoka's 12th regnal year.
  • Trap: The Barabar caves are associated with Ajivikas, not exclusively with Buddhism.

[Sources: NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 3, Arts of the Mauryan Period, p. 20; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Chapter 4, Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings, pp. 87 and 107; Archaeological Survey of India, Patna Circle, Monuments Details, entries 18–23, accessed 23 November 2026; Bihar Barabar Cave-Tourism, About Barabar Hill Caves, accessed 23 November 2026.]

title: Barabar Hills and Lomas Rishi: Early Mauryan Rock-cut Caves

body:
Location and religious association

The Ajanta Caves are a major Buddhist rock-cut complex in Maharashtra. They were excavated in a curved cliff above the Waghora River. The site contains both chaitya halls, which served religious worship, and viharas, which provided monastic accommodation.

Ajanta is particularly celebrated for the combination of architecture, sculpture and wall painting. Its paintings provide visual evidence of Buddhist religious narratives as well as aspects of life and society in ancient India.

Two major phases of construction

Excavation at Ajanta occurred in 2 important phases separated by several centuries.

Early phase: approximately 2nd–1st century BCE

The earlier excavations are associated with the Satavahana period. The architecture includes halls with stupas and comparatively simple monastic spaces. Caves 9 and 10 are notable early chaitya halls, while Caves 12 and 13 belong to the early monastic phase.

Later phase: approximately 5th–6th century CE

The later phase developed mainly under the Vakatakas and related regional patrons. Its caves are generally more elaborate, with developed sculptural programmes, shrines containing Buddha images and extensive paintings.

One identified patron was Varahadeva, a minister of the Vakataka ruler Harishena, associated with Cave 16. The association illustrates the role of patrons in the expansion of Buddhist monasteries.

Important cave numbers

The following associations help identify Ajanta's principal architectural and artistic features:

  • Caves 9 and 10: early chaitya halls.
  • Caves 19 and 26: later, more elaborately sculpted chaitya halls.
  • Caves 1 and 2: especially well-known for surviving paintings.
  • Caves 16 and 17: important surviving paintings and Buddhist narratives.
  • Cave 26: includes a monumental representation of the Buddha's Mahaparinirvana.

Why different sources give different cave counts

The UNESCO World Heritage Centre describes 30 caves at Ajanta, including unfinished examples, and identifies 5 chaityagrihas: Caves 9, 10, 19, 26 and 29. Cave 29 is unfinished. Some textbook accounts describe 29 caves and emphasise the 4 completed major chaitya halls. The difference is a matter of counting convention, not the existence of 2 separate cave sites.

Paintings and their subjects

Ajanta's wall paintings mainly represent events from the Buddha's life, Jataka stories and Avadana narratives. Jataka stories recount earlier births of the Buddha, often showing ideals such as compassion, generosity and sacrifice. Avadanas are Buddhist narratives that illustrate the consequences of actions and the value of meritorious conduct.

The paintings also depict palaces, processions, attendants, ornaments and everyday activities. These scenes help explain the social settings in which religious stories were represented.

Padmapani and Vajrapani

The famous paintings of Padmapani and Vajrapani in Cave 1 are among Ajanta's best-known images.

Padmapani is a form of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara, commonly recognised by the lotus. Vajrapani is associated with the vajra, an emblem traditionally linked with spiritual power. A Bodhisattva is a being who seeks enlightenment while acting for the welfare of other beings.

Jataka narratives

The Chaddanta Jataka, involving a noble elephant, appears in paintings associated with Caves 10 and 17. It is an example of how Buddhist stories were communicated visually across different periods of cave activity.

Why Ajanta is historically distinctive

Ajanta combines early stupa-centred worship spaces with later monasteries containing large images of the Buddha. It therefore helps illustrate changes in Buddhist art over time. Unlike Ellora, which includes monuments of 3 major religious traditions, Ajanta is fundamentally a Buddhist cave complex.

Ajanta was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1983.

Prelims focus

  • Ajanta: Maharashtra, above the Waghora River; Buddhist complex.
  • Early phase: approximately 2nd–1st century BCE, associated with Satavahana patronage.
  • Later phase: approximately 5th–6th century CE, associated with the Vakatakas.
  • Chaitya halls: Caves 9, 10, 19 and 26; UNESCO also includes unfinished Cave 29.
  • Cave 1: Padmapani and Vajrapani paintings.
  • Trap: Ajanta's murals and Buddhist caves should not be confused with Ellora's 3-faith cave complex.

[Sources: NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 4, Post-Mauryan Trends in Indian Art and Architecture, pp. 37–41; NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 12, Buildings, Paintings and Books, p. 126; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Chapter 4, Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings, pp. 102–103; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Ajanta Caves, Brief Synthesis and Outstanding Universal Value, accessed 23 November 2026.]
